title: The Pattern-Seeking Fallacy: why mining marketing data for "insights" finds noise
summary: Humans see patterns in randomness, and slicing analytics or A/B test data many ways guarantees some "significant" result appears by chance. Jason Cohen argues you should form a theory first, then test that specific theory, rather than hunting through combinations after the fact.

principles.text: Humans are bad at telling real patterns from randomness, even when trying to be analytical.
principles.quote: We humans are terrible at discerning patterns from randomness, and in marketing data we unwittingly find "insights" that are actually noise.

principles.text: Combing a mountain of data for a pattern guarantees you will find one, and it means nothing.
principles.quote: This is the epitome of Pattern-Seeking--combing through a mountain of data until you find a pattern.

principles.text: Rare events become inevitable when you run enough trials, so a striking result from many comparisons isn't evidence.
principles.quote: Those events are rare, but I'm flipping so much that rare events will naturally occur.

principles.text: Slicing analytics many ways is like running 1000 coin-flip trials and reporting only the all-heads one.
principles.quote: Except you're running 1000 coin-flip trials, looking only at the trial where it came up all heads and declaring the coin "biased."

principles.text: Use apparent patterns to form a theory, then test it deliberately; don't treat the pattern as the insight.
principles.quote: You can use apparent patterns to form a theory; that's good. [...] But then you have to test it, so that it's science, not baseball announcing.

principles.text: Decide beforehand which metrics and cohorts matter, and test a specific hypothesis instead of generating many ad variants.
principles.quote: Instead of rooting around Google Analytics hoping to find a combination of factors with a good conversion rate, decide beforehand which conversion rates are important for which cohorts, then measure and track those only.
